name: Manobo, Ata
confidence_why: No source says where Ata Manobo stress falls: Reid 1971 relays an unpublished 1964 SIL phonology by Morey and Post that lists stress as a phoneme without giving its position, Zorc 1978 and Lobel 2013 remark only in passing that Manobo and most Mindanao languages have lost contrastive accent, and Austin 1966, the SIL grammatical papers of Hartung and Abbott, and the 2016 dictionary are silent.

catalog_quote: Stress: Genny Morey notes that the basic word stess [sic] of Ata consists of primary stress on the penult or atepenult [sic] of a word and secondary stress on the ultima: gísì? 'to tear', nágisì? 'torn', ogkágisì? 'may be torn', and so forth. When a word is emphasized the emphasis consists of a reversal of the primary and secondary stress placement: gìsí? 'to tear', nàgisí? 'torn', ogkàgisí? 'may be torn', kànák 'me' and so forth [indented:] primary stress indicated by acute accent and seconday [sic] stress by grave in these examples. [circled:] Orthography: l [underlined] the l exists in upriver dialects but not in ours / glottal stop is marked either as - or ? / ng represents /ŋ/

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reid's phoneme inventory for Ata Manobo (after Morey & Post's unpublished analysis) lists 'Stress' as a phoneme, i.e. word stress is treated as contrastive/unpredictable, but stress was not marked on the printed word list and no statement of its usual position is given. This conflicts with the comparative literature (Zorc 1977/1978: Manobo languages 'have lost contrastive accent'; Lobel 2013 fn.3) and no accessible first-hand Ata Manobo description states where stress falls. Austin 1966's phonology summary lists only 19 segmental phonemes and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None recoverable; Reid's note concerns only the down-river vs up-river l : zero dialect difference.
new_statements.domain_note: Phoneme-chart listing only (word-level phonemic stress asserted by inclusion in the inventory); no discussion of word vs phrase domain or citation forms. Evidence is second-hand (Reid compiling an unpublished SIL manuscript) and was read only through search snippets, not a saved page scan.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Ata Manobo [atd] = atam1240 ('Ata of Davao', 'Langilan'), specifically the 'down-river' dialect around Mansalinao on the Liboganon River (Reid 1971 note; Webonary introduction); Reid records an up-river vs down-river l : zero difference and Hartung 1967 calls Tigwa Manobo (Glottolog: under Matigsalug mati1250) mutually intelligible. Not to be confused with the Ata (Negrito) language of Negros Island, nor with the short SIL 'Aeta of Davao' word list, whose forms (otaw 'person', dakel 'big', -enno verbs) do not look like Ata Manobo. The Dibabawon Manobo (mbd) penultimate-pitch statement in Forster & Barnard 1987 is a neighbouring language and must not be attributed to atam1240.

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing tension stands unchanged: Reid 1971 (relaying Morey & Post's unpublished 1963/64 phonology) lists 'Stress (not indicated on list)' in the Ata Manobo phoneme chart, implying contrastive stress with no placement rule, while Zorc 1977/1978 and Lobel 2013 state generally that Manobo languages have lost contrastive accent; Austin's summary of the same Morey & Post ms gives only 19 segmental phonemes and no stress phoneme, which leans slightly toward the 'no contrastive stress' side but is an argument from silence in a syntax/discourse thesis.
